title: “East of Eden” Is at the Library; Now It Comes to TV | Timeless

text:
Florence Pugh and Zoe Kazan, the star and screenwriter (respectively) of Netflix’s “East of Eden,” a fresh take on John Steinbeck’s classic 1952 California novel, recently came to the Library to get a look at some original Steinbeck material.

Among other items on display, there were signed first editions of “Eden,” manuscript pages from “The Grapes of Wrath” and a dozen or so books from the 19 th and early 20 th centuries that documented the land and the people of the Salinas Valley, the primary setting of “Eden,” “Of Mice and Men” and other Steinbeck works.

The seven-episode series, which debuts tomorrow, will stretch, like the book, from the end of the Civil War to World War I. It will also be a tale of good and evil, like the book, but is more centered around the lightning rod character of Cathy Ames, played by Pugh.

“I believe there are monsters born in the world to human parents,” Steinbeck writes in introducing Cathy in the novel, a famous sentence that also begins the series’ trailer, already viewed more than 5 million times on YouTube alone.

“There was a time when a girl like Cathy would have been called possessed by the devil,” he continues a few paragraphs later. “She would have been exorcised to cast out the evil spirit, and if after many trials that did not work, she would have been burned as a witch for the good of the community.”

How the series plays out will be Kazan’s telling, but as the granddaughter of the director Elia Kazan, who filmed “Eden” in 1955 — the movie that made James Dean a star — she has thought about it for a long time. She read the book as a teen and loved it, well before seeing her grandfather’s film version. (Steinbeck gave her grandfather one of the signed, limited editions of the book, and she was thrilled to see another copy in the rare, original slipcase at the Library.)

She started the screenplay six years ago, she recently told Vanity Fair , and was transfixed with Cathy.

“There’s a real clarity to the quality of her selfishness, which I found completely fascinating,” she said. “… Her agency was so strong, and she kind of took over the book.”

Steinbeck considered “Eden” to be his magnum opus even before he wrote it.

“I have written each book as an exercise, as practice for the one to come,” he wrote the day before he started work on the novel, in “Journal of a Novel: The ‘East of Eden’ Letters.” (His journal was not intended for publication, and it was released only after his death in 1968.) “And this is the one to come. There is nothing beyond this book — nothing follows it. It must contain all in the world I know and it must have everything in it of which I am capable …”

It was not a surprise, then, that the multigenerational tale of the Hamilton and Trask families ran to 602 pages. It was also not a surprise that given its melodrama and repeated first-person, philosophical observations by Steinbeck, that critical reviews were bitterly divided.

Its popular appeal, though, was never in doubt — the book quickly went to No. 1 on bestseller lists and has never been out of print. The Netflix version will be at least the third time it has been filmed, both for television and cinema, and there have been many stage productions.

It was based on Steinbeck’s family history in California, most particularly that stretch around Monterey and down through the Salinas Valley, now generally known as “Steinbeck country.” He wrote it, he said, for his two young sons to read later so they would understand not only their family background, but everything he had learned about people and human society. He considered it so profound that he modeled it on the Cain and Abel story in the Biblical book of Genesis.

When he was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1962, the Nobel committee most prominently cited “The Grapes of Wrath” (which had won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award) and “Of Mice and Men,” but also cited “Eden” and “The Pearl” as major works.

In his “Journal,” he was painfully self-conscious that he was attempting to write the work of a lifetime. It gave him fits.

“Lord, this is a difficult book,” he wrote on Friday, Feb. 25, 1951, about three weeks into the writing. “I hope I can keep all the reins in my hands and at the same time make it sound as though the book were almost accidental. That is going to be hard to do but it must be done. Also I’ll have to lead into the story so gradually that my reader will not know what is happening to him until he is caught.”

Some 75 years later, readers (and viewers) are still transfixed.
